live_cases.name: University of Tennessee Research Foundation v. Anthropic PBC

case.why_ai_cites_it: The first machine-authorship case, and the template both sides use. AI companies and their users cite it for the claim that prompting, curating and arranging make a human the author of machine-assisted output; opponents cite it for the premise that authorship requires a human making the creative choices at all.

reading.body:
The clearest precedent AI copyright disputes reach for is a nineteenth-century photograph case, and the reason is that its core question, who made the creative choices, is exactly the question generative AI reopens.

In 1884 the Supreme Court held that a photographer could hold copyright because posing, lighting, and arranging the subject expressed the photographer's own judgment. The camera was a tool; the human behind it was the author. AI companies and their users now borrow that logic to argue that prompting and curating AI output is the same kind of expressive selection. Opponents borrow the same case to argue the opposite: that Sarony matters precisely because a human made every creative decision, and a generative model making choices of its own breaks that chain.

The data notes the limit plainly. Sarony involved a scene a human staged in full, while a generative model contributes expressive choices that are not reducible to the operator's instructions. How much human selection is sufficient is being resolved case by case, by the Copyright Office and the courts, and this 1884 holding tells readers where that line-drawing started, not where it will end. One live case, University of Tennessee Research Foundation v. Anthropic, is the only current litigation the data connects to this precedent, so the record here covers the doctrinal origin and one downstream dispute, nothing more.
